capabilities.target: User's home directory, C:/Users/dev, mounted whole (includes ~/.aws/credentials)
Third-party quicknotes hosted sync service (author-controlled), via the 'context' argument
Any Slack channel, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User request typed into the desktop client
Tool names and descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp's tools/list response
Content returned by quicknotes_mcp (notes data / hosted sync service responses)

controls.name: Desktop client first-call tool approval, cached as 'always allow'
controls.decay_rationale: Approval is requested once per tool name and then cached as 'always allow'; it does not re-prompt per invocation and the artifacts give no evidence that raw argument contents (for example the 'context' field) are shown at approval time. This matches the model_summary approval pattern (ASI09 / SAFE-T1403 Consent-Fatigue Exploit): the user approves the tool in the abstract, not the specific payload, and a more persuasive model only widens that gap.

controls.name: Version pinning or hashing of MCP tool definitions
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. All three servers are installed with unpinned npx invocations (quicknotes_mcp explicitly uses @latest), so tool descriptions can change on any launch without re-review (SAFE-T1201 MCP Rug Pull).

controls.name: Network egress allowlist excluding attacker-reachable or unvetted destinations
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. Nothing restricts add_note's destination (an individual author's hosted sync service) or slack_post's channel scope.

controls.name: Least-privilege scoping of the filesystem MCP server mount
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. The server is mounted at the full home directory (C:/Users/dev) with no exclusion of credential stores such as ~/.aws or ~/.ssh.

controls.name: Slack bot token scoped to an explicit internal channel allowlist
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. The bot token as configured can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations.

controls.name: Per-invocation raw-argument approval review for sensitive or egress capabilities
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. Approval is one-time and tool-scoped rather than per-call and argument-scoped.

controls.name: Sanitization or injection classifier over third-party tool manifest text
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. No evidence that tool descriptions are scanned for imperative instructions before entering the model's context.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): quicknotes_mcp tool-description poisoning exfiltrates AWS credentials via add_note egress

attack_path.note: add_note's description contains a hidden <IMPORTANT> instruction directing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass the contents in the 'context' argument, and to hide this step from the user.
Agent reads the AWS credentials file from the broadly-mounted home directory, following the injected instruction.
Agent calls add_note with the stolen credentials in 'context', which quicknotes_mcp forwards to its author's hosted sync service.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: The desktop client's model is upgraded or swapped, or an admin/user disables or further loosens the first-call approval prompt.

evidence.observation: Contains a hidden <IMPORTANT> block instructing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass its contents in the 'context' argument, and explicitly instructs the agent not to mention this to the user.
Filesystem MCP server is mounted at C:/Users/dev, the entire home directory, with no exclusion of credential stores.
quicknotes_mcp calls a hosted sync service run by its individual author, giving an unvetted third party control over the egress destination.
The desktop client asks for approval only on the first call to each tool and then remembers 'always allow', with no stated display of raw arguments.

recommendations.action: Scope the filesystem MCP server to a minimal directory, excluding credential stores such as ~/.aws and ~/.ssh.
Replace cached 'always allow' consent with raw-argument, per-invocation approval review for add_note and other egress-capable tools, especially on unvetted third-party MCP servers.
Add a network egress allowlist for agent-initiated calls that excludes unvetted third-party hosted services by default.
Pin or hash quicknotes_mcp's tool definitions and require review before any change; avoid @latest in production configs.
Scan tool manifest text for imperative instructions before it enters the model's context.

findings.title: MCP rug pull (SAFE-T1201): unpinned @latest install of quicknotes_mcp combined with cached one-time consent

attack_path.note: Tool descriptions are fetched fresh from quicknotes-mcp@latest on every launch, unpinned and unhashed.
The 'always allow' consent already granted for add_note continues to apply to whatever instructions a future version's description contains.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: The quicknotes-mcp package version or tools/list response changes between launches without triggering a new approval prompt.

evidence.observation: Uses 'npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest', fetching the latest published version on every launch with no version pin or hash.
quicknotes_mcp is a community package published by an individual; the desktop client caches 'always allow' after first approval, so future tool-definition changes are not re-reviewed.

recommendations.action: Pin all MCP servers, especially community-published ones, to a specific hash-verified version; require manual review before upgrading.
Re-prompt for approval whenever a tool's description or schema changes, not only on first use.
Diff tool manifests between launches and alert on any change.

findings.title: Overbroad Slack bot scope creates a second lethal-trifecta egress path (TC1 variant) into externally-shared channels

attack_path.note: quicknotes_mcp has already demonstrated the ability to embed hidden imperative instructions in tool descriptions loaded into the agent's context.
Agent can read sensitive local files, including credentials or other documents, under the home directory.
The Slack bot token can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, giving a second, broadly-scoped egress sink.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: A hidden instruction in any tool description that targets slack.post_message directly, or removal/weakening of the first-call approval gate.

evidence.observation: The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, i.e. the credential scope is broad rather than least-privilege.

Demonstrates this untrusted input source already embeds hidden imperative instructions aimed at the agent, establishing the same mechanism could target other reachable tools such as slack.post_message.
SLACK_BOT_TOKEN is injected via environment variable with no indication of channel-level scoping.

recommendations.action: Scope the Slack bot token to an explicit allowlist of internal channels, excluding channels shared with external organizations.
Bind message destinations to a system-of-record channel list rather than a model-chosen channel argument.
Apply the same raw-argument, per-invocation approval review recommended for add_note to slack.post_message.

findings.title: Forecast: memory laundering (TC5) if quicknotes note content is later read back into Slack summaries

attack_path.note: Content returned by the third-party hosted sync service, authored/controlled by the quicknotes_mcp author, currently has no declared reachability into other capabilities.
Hypothetical future feature in which the agent reads back prior notes to compose Slack updates, at which point this untrusted content would be treated as internal and trusted.

forecast.watch_signal: The agent gains a feature that reads quicknotes note content back into context to compose outbound Slack messages or other egress.

evidence.observation: quicknotes_mcp calls a hosted sync service run by its author, so notes content is not declared as reachable into any other capability today, but the same author already controls injected instructions returned to the agent.

recommendations.action: If a future feature reads quicknotes content back into context, tag it as untrusted (U) and require it to pass the same injection checks as any other third-party input before it can reach an egress capability.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical because an untrusted, attacker-controlled input (quicknotes_mcp's own tool description) already demonstrates the ability to direct the agent to read restricted credential data and move it across a trust boundary via add_note, with Slack's broad channel scope offering a second egress sink, and autonomy fields show no step or runtime caps. Residual risk is moderate across all present-horizon findings because the only preventive control, a first-call-then-cached approval gate, earns the rubric's standard -2 tier credit but is floored at moderate: it was declared without evidence that it shows raw arguments (approval_review_mode: model_summary), and in practice the 'always allow' cache means it does not re-examine the very call that carries the poisoned payload. No other structural containment (egress allowlist, scoped filesystem mount, scoped Slack token, definition pinning) is present, so there is nothing to credit at rubric steps 1, 3, or 4. The forecast returns to critical because the approval gate is exactly the kind of model_summary, partially_dependent control that control_decay.md identifies as failing under model_upgrade or simple control_removal; once it is defeated, no other control stands between the untrusted tool description and either egress capability. The single control whose decay moves the forecast most is ctrl.first_call_approval.

output_consumers: Slack channel members, including external organizations

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and the runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.
No system prompt or agent instructions were provided, so behavioral/prompt-level controls could not be assessed and are treated as absent.

The desktop client's approval-dialog UI (whether it shows raw arguments or only a tool name) was not provided as an artifact; approval_review_mode is conservatively scored as model_summary per rubric default, which limits confidence in the exact residual tier.

The exact data content normally read by fs.read_file and posted via slack.post_message in day-to-day use was not specified; sensitivity classifications are inferred from the home-directory scope and channel breadth described in the runtime notes.
